biggestWin: Compose the first-run hero card. Today it is 1084x269 holding 357px of content: the figure column, then a 57px column with a 57px stub of baseline, then 629px of unclaimed white inside the card border — 58% of the card. It is the state every new owner meets first and it is the only place on this surface where the layout reads as inherited rather than composed. Constrain the card to its content in that state (two CSS rules, no restructure, no faint slots, no widened ruler) and the weakest composition on the page becomes a deliberate one.

findings.element: .plot .gridline b (top gridline label) and .plot .bar-val, chart in movementOne
findings.problem: The chart's top gridline value is Math.round(max) where max = Math.max(D.peak, D.bestPrior), and D.peak includes the live week. Whenever the running week is the tallest of the twelve — which is the shipped fixture and the case the chart most wants to show — the axis ceiling and the live week's value are the same number, and both are printed just above the plot's top edge, right-aligned to two different rails 34px apart. Driven in chromium at every width from 360 to 1600 in 20px steps, in states full, partial and quiet, on both grounds: the two label boxes overlap vertically by 8.0px with a horizontal gap of 14.8px, so the top-right of the chart reads '12 SO FAR  12' in one 11px tracked uppercase mono line. The two are not on a shared baseline either — the bar-val sits 6.9px higher and floats clear of the gridline while the axis label straddles it, so the pair reads as a typographic accident rather than as two labels on a rail. In dark the separation is weaker still: Indigo 400 against Ink 3 on Ground puts the two at near-identical luminance. This is not the closed r1 'bar-val-overprints-axis-max' — the 34px gutter that closed it is working and the boxes do not intersect. The defect is that the surface prints one number twice, 15px apart, meaning two different things.
findings.consequence: The reader's eye goes to the top-right of the chart to read the live week, which is the one figure the whole card is built to deliver, and lands on a duplicated numeral it must parse before it can trust: is the second 12 part of the sentence, a second count, or the ceiling? It costs the most-read corner of the surface a beat of doubt for no information — the axis top is already stated by the live mark that reaches it.
findings.fix: In chart(), suppress the numeral on the g=1 gridline when it duplicates the live week's printed value. Replace the grid builder with: const live = D.weeks.length ? D.weeks[D.weeks.length - 1].v : null; const grid = [0.5, 1].map((g) => { const v = Math.round(max * g); const dup = g === 1 && v === live; return `${dup ? "" : `${v}`}`; }).join(""); The gridline itself still draws — only its numeral goes, and only when the live mark already prints that number at that height in a stronger voice. Nothing about the gutter, the rails or the record tag moves, and on any fixture where the live week is not the peak both labels return unchanged. Note that this deliberately breaks interaction-check.mjs line 258, 'the chart states its own scale' (grid.top asserts the gridline labels include max(weeks)); amend it to accept the maximum being stated by either a .gridline b or the .bar-val, so the assertion still fails if the scale goes unstated entirely.
findings.assertion: At ?state=full|partial|quiet, v=light and dark, at every configured viewport: collect the text of every .plot .gridline b and every .plot .bar-val; no numeral appears in both sets. And, generalising the existing overprint check at interaction-check.mjs:653 so it can catch this class rather than only strict intersection: for every pair of chart labels whose boxes overlap vertically by more than 0px, the horizontal gap between them must exceed 24px (one rung).

findings.problem: The hero card keeps the full-state two-column grid — minmax(220px,300px) 1fr — while its second column holds a plot narrowed to 57px. Measured in chromium at 1440: card 1084x268.9; figure column 231->531; chart column 579->1265 with .cols, .baseline and the ruler all clamped to 579->636. From the right edge of the only painted mark to the card's inner edge is 629px of unclaimed white, 58% of the card, with nothing drawn in it — not even the axis, because .plot.solo .baseline is narrowed to 57px too, so the floor stops as a 57px stub. At 1280 the same 629px. At 900 and below the hero stacks and the card becomes 483.8px tall with a 698px chart row holding 57px of mark and a 641px void; at 390, 251px of void in a 467.8px-tall card. The column pitch and the narrow ruler are both argued in source and both closed in earlier rounds — this finding does not touch either. The card's width is the part nothing argues.
findings.consequence: First-run is the state a brand-new owner sees before any other, and the hero — the object that carries the whole answer — presents as a broken grid: a figure, a hairline mark, and half a card of blank paper. It reads as a page that failed to load its right half, which is the opposite of what a first reading should say, and it is the only composition on this surface that reads as unfinished rather than deliberate.
findings.fix: Two rules, keyed off the state attribute the body already carries, so the pitch, the honest-degradation contract and the r2 ruler fix are all untouched: `[data-state="first-run"] .hero { grid-template-columns: minmax(220px, 300px) auto; }` and `[data-state="first-run"] .card.hero { max-width: 460px; }`. At 1440/1280 the card becomes 24+300+48+57+24 = 453px of content in a 460px box, left-aligned on the page's column edge, with a short right edge against the full-width bands below it — a stated 'there is not much here yet' rather than a void. At 900 and below the existing stacked grid takes over and max-width 460 still holds the card to its content; at 390 the 342px page width already binds and nothing changes. No slot, no scale and no widened ruler is introduced, so nothing claims eleven weeks of zero.
findings.assertion: At ?state=first-run, both grounds, at 390/768/900/1280/1440: the distance from the right edge of .plot.solo .baseline to the inner right edge of .card.hero (its right minus its padding-right) is <= 48px, one rung; equivalently .card.hero's width is within two rungs of the width its painted content occupies. The check must fail against the current build, where that distance is 629px at 1440.

findings.problem: The assertion is named 'the first-run mark's height comes from its value, not a literal' and its comment names the class it guards: 'a mark whose height is a typed literal encodes nothing'. Its test is `plot.h === 100`, where plot.h is read straight off `bar.style.getPropertyValue("--h")` — and the first-run template in lately.html writes that attribute as the literal `--h:100`. The evaluate also reads `value: f.weeks[f.weeks.length - 1].v` into the returned object and then never compares it to anything. Proven, not inferred: I drove ?state=first-run in chromium with an addInitScript setter that rewrites the fixture's live week to 3 before the surface renders. The hero printed 3, the mark printed '3 so far', the spoken line said 3 — and --h was still 100, the bar still painted 168px in a 168px plot, and the assertion still returned PASS. It cannot fail for any fixture value. It asserts the literal equals the literal, and it certifies the exact condition its own name says it forbids. This is the fifth vacuous assertion in this gate and it sits on a state protected by a closed r1 finding.
findings.consequence: A closed r1 defect on the state every new owner meets first is guarded by a check that cannot fail, so the count of green assertions overstates what is actually held down. The person using the product is exposed indirectly but really: if the first-run mark's height ever decouples from its value, 461 assertions pass and nobody is told.
findings.fix: Delete the tautology and assert the relations that can fail. Replace the three lines with: (a) the printed mark reads the fixture's live week — `document.querySelector('.bar-val').textContent.trim() === `${F.weeks.at(-1).v} so far``; (b) the hero numeral reads the same value; (c) the mark's painted height equals the plot's painted height within 1px, since a solo week is its own maximum — this fails the moment the literal is edited to anything but 100; and (d) the source guard the comment intends: read lately.html and assert the first-run bar's --h is written as an interpolation of D, not as a bare digit — `!/class="bar part" style="--h:\s*\d/.test(src)`. Write (d) to a file with an editor and verify it against both the current source (must fail) and the corrected source (must pass) before it lands. Keep 'the first-run mark stands at a real column's width' but bind it to the pitch rather than to a 60px ceiling it can never breach: assert the mark's width equals a .colw's max-width in the full state's chart.
findings.assertion: The replacement block must be observed FAILING against the current build before it is accepted — specifically (d) against lately.html as it stands, and (a)/(c) under a fixture whose live week is forced to a value other than the drawn one. An assertion added to this gate that has never been seen red is an untested claim (lessons.md L-05, L-06).

findings.problem: The three composed-alike terminal blocks all use .center with gap: var(--gap-line). In empty and quiet the heading and its body are separate flex children, so the rung applies: measured at 1440, empty h2 bottom 327.9 -> p top 343.9 = 16.0px; quiet head 763.5 -> body 779.5 = 16.0px. In error both the h2 and the p live inside `<div role="alert">`, which is itself the single flex child, so the gap lands between the alert and the button and never between the heading and its explanation: h2 bottom 327.9 -> p top 327.9 = 0.0px. Every other spacing in the block is identical (padding-top 72, heading-to-button 24 in both states), so this is the one gap on the surface that is not a rung on the declared ladder — and it is zero because a wrapper swallowed it, not because anyone chose it. audit.mjs reads the source for raw px in margin, padding and gap, and interaction-check.mjs:625 checks margins are rungs; a gap that simply does not apply is invisible to both.
findings.consequence: The state a person meets when the product has failed them is the one state whose headline and explanation are set flush, so it reads tighter and more anxious than the empty and quiet states it is supposed to match. It is a small thing that lands at the worst moment, and it is the only place where this surface's own spacing discipline slips.
findings.fix: Give the alert wrapper the rung the flex child it replaced would have had: `.center [role="alert"] { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: var(--gap-line); }`. Nothing else moves — the wrapper stays for the live-region semantics, the heading-to-button distance stays at 24px, and the empty and quiet states are untouched.
findings.assertion: At ?state=error and ?state=empty, both grounds, at 390/768/1280/1440: the vertical distance from the state h2's bottom to the top of the paragraph that follows it is 16px in both states, and the two numbers are equal. Generalise it: in every terminal block, every vertical gap between adjacent text blocks is a member of the ladder [4,8,12,16,24,32,48,72].

findings.problem: The denominator card is composed as a portrait tile: a label, a 34px numeral and a phrase, stacked. At 1440 that is exactly right — 204x156.6, ink filling 57.1% of its inner width, and its area is 1.00x a sibling's. Below 900 the row goes two-up and the lead card spans both columns, but its contents do not change: the identical 98.3x86.8 ink block now sits in a 748x125.5 plate at 900 (13.7% of its inner width), 616x125.5 at 768 (16.8%), 342x125.5 at 390 (31.7%). The plate's area becomes 1.88x a sibling's at 900 and 768 and 1.68x at 390 — and it is the only solid-ink object in the band. Nothing composed that box; it is what grid-column: 1 / -1 did to a tile designed portrait.
findings.consequence: On phone and tablet the first and heaviest object in 'What's quietly slipping' is a large black banner that is five-sixths empty and carries the context rather than the finding. The eye lands on the denominator before any of the four counts the movement exists to deliver, so the band's reading order inverts at exactly the widths the audience uses most.
findings.fix: Lay the plate out as a banner where it is shaped like one, inside the existing <=900 media query: `.kpi.lead { flex-direction: row; align-items: baseline; gap: var(--gap-snug); } .kpi.lead > .t-label { height: auto; } .kpi.lead > .t-small { flex: 0 0 auto; }`. 'Open now  9  jobs not finished' then sets on one line, the plate drops to roughly 66px tall and its area returns to about 1.0x a sibling's, so it reads as the row's stated denominator rather than as its dominant object. The shared-denominator contract is untouched: the same 9, in the same card, in the same row. The kpi-row-shares-one-line assertions at interaction-check.mjs:711 run only at 1280 and 1440, where the row is five-across, so nothing existing conflicts.
findings.assertion: At ?state=full and ?state=partial, at 390/560/768/900, both grounds: the area of .kpi.lead is no more than 1.25x the area of the largest other .kpi in the row, and its painted ink spans at least 40% of its own inner width. The check must fail against the current build, where the ratio is 1.88x and the ink spans 13.7% at 900.
